questiontext.text: What is the main purpose of an Ansible inventory?

generalfeedback.text: Inventory identifies target hosts and groups and can associate variables such as SSH connection details with them.

answer.text: To store a binary snapshot of every server
To replace all role defaults and templates
To identify managed hosts and groups, with variables such as connection details
To record only the commands that previously failed

questiontext.text: A playbook ensures that Nginx is installed but says nothing about an unrelated package installed manually. What should you generally expect?

generalfeedback.text: Ansible ordinarily manages the state expressed by the tasks. An omitted resource is not automatically declared absent; additional unmanaged state can remain.

answer.text: The unrelated package remains unless a task explicitly manages or removes it.
Ansible removes every package absent from the playbook.
Ansible recreates the server from a stock image.
The playbook must fail because the server has additional state.

generalfeedback.text: Roles organize related tasks, defaults, templates, handlers, and other supporting resources into reusable units. They do not guarantee task parallelism or prohibit shared variables.

answer.text: Roles guarantee that all tasks run simultaneously.
Each role creates its own independent Ansible installation.
Roles prevent the use of variables shared across hosts.
Roles package related tasks and supporting files so they can be organized and reused.

questiontext.text: Consider a simplified version of the demo's port configuration using a scalar variable named app_port. Role defaults set it to 8080, the target host's group variables set it to 3000, and the playbook command includes -e app_port=9000. What value should {{ app_port }} produce?

generalfeedback.text:
The command-line extra variable sets app_port to 9000. Extra variables have higher variable precedence than the group variables and role defaults in this example. Multiple definitions are permitted; precedence determines the effective value. The scalar form in the question avoids unrelated dictionary-merging details.

Technical reference: Ansible variable precedence.

answer.text: 8080, because the role owns its configuration
9000, because the extra variable overrides the other supplied values
3000, because group variables always override command-line values
An error, because the same variable cannot appear in multiple places

name.text: L3 Q5 Selecting hosts and roles

questiontext.text: In demo-03a/provisioning/provision.yml, the common role targets fleet, while the web, database, and batch roles target their respective host groups. Explain which roles a host belonging to web_servers should receive and why the grouping is useful.

graderinfo.text:
• 1 mark: A web host belongs to web_servers, which is a child group of fleet, so it receives the common role in the first play and the web role in the web play during a normal full run.
  • 1 mark: This applies a shared baseline to the fleet while limiting specialized configuration to the appropriate hosts. It avoids installing the entire database or batch stack everywhere.

questiontext.text: Explain the difference between state: started and enabled: yes in a service task. Why is state: restarted different from state: started when a playbook is run repeatedly?

graderinfo.text:
• 1 mark: state: started requests that the service be running now, while enabled: yes requests that it start automatically at boot. These are distinct aspects of service state.
  • 1 mark: state: restarted requests a restart whenever the task executes, whereas state: started normally leaves an already running service running. Repeated restart operations can cause unnecessary disruption even if the final service state is “running.”

questiontext.text:
The infrastructure playbook in demo-03a uses:

- name: Create web security group
  amazon.aws.ec2_security_group:
    # Other settings omitted
    state: present
  register: web_sg

# A later EC2 task uses:
# security_group: "{{ web_sg.group_id }}"

Explain what register does here and why the later task uses the returned group ID instead of a manually copied value. These are excerpts; no execution is required.

graderinfo.text:
• 1 mark: register: web_sg stores the task's returned result in a variable named web_sg, including its group_id.
  • 1 mark: Referencing that returned ID passes the actual created or located resource into the later task and avoids manually duplicating a changing cloud identifier. The producing task must execute before its result is consumed in this sequence.

questiontext.text: The demo separates 00_create.sh, 50_provision.sh, and 60_test.sh. Explain the difference between creating infrastructure and provisioning its operating-system/application state. Why is a separate functional test useful even when provisioning exits successfully?

graderinfo.text:
• 1 mark: Creation establishes infrastructure such as instances, security groups, and connection information; provisioning installs/configures the operating-system and application resources on those instances.
  • 1 mark: Successful tasks do not prove that the application works end to end. Functional tests can check health endpoints, database access, or communication between components that might still be misconfigured.

questiontext.text:
Consider this shortened excerpt from the web role in demo-03a:

# tasks/main.yml
- name: Configure Nginx for web application
  template:
    src: nginx-site.conf.j2
    dest: /etc/nginx/sites-available/{{ project_name }}
  notify:
    - reload nginx

# handlers/main.yml
- name: reload nginx
  systemd:
    name: nginx
    state: reloaded

Assume a successful play, no forced handler flushes, and no other task notifying this handler.

  1. When should the handler run if rendering the template changes the destination file? What happens on the next run if the rendered file is identical? (2 marks)
  2. Suppose three changed tasks notify the same handler before the normal end-of-tasks handler phase. How many times should it run in that phase, and why is this useful? (2 marks)

graderinfo.text:
• 1 mark: A changed template task notifies reload nginx; in the stated scenario it runs at the normal handler phase after the play's regular tasks.
  • 1 mark: If the rendered file is unchanged on the next run, that task does not notify the handler, so it does not cause a reload.
  • 1 mark: The same handler runs once in that handler phase despite three notifications.
  • 1 mark: Combining notifications avoids redundant reloads and lets the service consume the completed configuration changes together.

Technical reference: Ansible handlers and notification timing. A later explicit flush or later handler phase changes the scope of the “once” statement; the question intentionally excludes that complication.

name.text: L3 Q10 A misleading idempotence guard

questiontext.text:
The web role contains this dependency-installation task:

- name: Install Node.js dependencies
  shell: |
    cd "{{ app_directory }}"
    npm install
  become_user: "{{ app_user }}"
  args:
    creates: "{{ app_directory }}/node_modules"

The node_modules directory already exists from an earlier deployment. A new application release changes the required dependencies in package.json.

  1. Predict whether this task runs and explain the resulting risk. (2 marks)
  2. Propose a change-aware way to install updated dependencies and one check that would show the application has the intended dependency state. Simply forcing every task to report ok is not a solution. (2 marks)

graderinfo.text:
• 1 mark: The existing node_modules path causes creates to skip the shell command.
  • 1 mark: Directory existence does not prove that installed dependencies match the new manifest; the application can retain stale or missing dependencies.
  • 1 mark: Propose a manifest/lockfile-aware installation step, for example register changes to deployed dependency definitions and run a suitable installation task when those change or dependencies are missing. A committed lockfile with npm ci is one valid approach, if the required files and installation conditions are handled correctly. A checksummed build artifact is another defensible approach.
  • 1 mark: Verify installed dependency versions against the intended manifest/lockfile or run a targeted application/smoke test that exercises the changed dependency. A combination is strongest. Merely testing whether the directory exists does not establish dependency correctness.

Technical references: Ansible shell creates guard and npm ci requirements.
